why contract state on a transparent chain is public even when a language marks it private: full nodes hold it, so anyone can read it from the chain's state or reconstruct it from transaction history, while visibility keywords limit only what code can access through the language; on many platforms other contracts read a contract's state only through what its code exposes, while off-chain observers can read all of it, so a secret has to stay off-chain, be encrypted, or be committed to as a hash that includes enough randomness that the value cannot be guessed

the split between persistent state, which outlives the invocation and is what later invocations read, and working data that lasts only for one invocation, or on some platforms one transaction; why anything a contract must remember between invocations has to be written to persistent state, which on metered platforms is often among the most expensive things it can do

why a contract's code and its data persist independently: when the logic acting on existing data is replaced, as behind a proxy, the new code inherits data written under the old code's layout and has to interpret it compatibly, and when a contract is replaced by a new one, its state stays with the old account unless it is moved explicitly

how an invocation enters a contract's code and selects what to run: on some platforms the contract's own code, typically generated by its compiler, reads an identifier at the start of the input, such as a function selector derived from the function's signature, and decodes the arguments, running a default path, if the contract defines one, for input that matches no function or carries only value, while on others the runtime calls an exported entry point by name; why the input encoding is an interface caller and callee have to share, and what a mismatch does, such as reaching the default path or failing

what a running invocation can draw on, namely its own state, the call's input, what its execution environment supplies, including on some platforms facts about other accounts such as their balances, and what the calls it makes return, and why anything else, such as an off-chain price, has to arrive through one of those channels from some party, so the contract's conclusions carry the trust placed in whoever supplied it

why, on platforms where code runs only when a transaction or another contract invokes it, such as Ethereum, a contract runs only inside invocations, and what that means for rules that depend on time: a deadline or expiry takes effect only when someone next invokes the contract and its code checks the condition, and an action due at a certain time needs an external caller, such as a keeper paid to invoke it, unless the platform itself schedules invocations

how one invocation ends and what its ending settles for that invocation alone: returning output with its state changes kept, provisionally wherever an enclosing execution can still fail, or failing, by reverting, so that its changes are discarded and error data is handed back, or by halting on an error it did not choose, such as exhausting its resources, which also discards its changes and on some platforms hands back no data; why, where the invocation is nested in a larger synchronous execution, a successful return settles nothing beyond the invocation, since the enclosing execution can still fail and discard its changes

how one contract invokes another across platforms: synchronously, with the caller suspended until the callee returns within the same execution and the result usable at once, or asynchronously, with a message delivered and executed later, possibly in another block, shard or chain, while the caller continues, so the caller cannot use the result in the same step and the state it acted on may have changed by the time a reply arrives

how failure crosses a call boundary: in a synchronous call, on platforms that let the caller observe the failure, the caller either propagates the callee's failure, so its own work is undone with it, or handles the failure and continues with its own changes kept; in an asynchronous design the caller's changes may already be committed before the failure is known, so the failure arrives, if the design reports it at all, as a later reply or returned message and the caller has to reverse its own effects with explicit compensating steps

what a call target binds and what it does not: a caller names an address and an expected interface, but the code at that address decides what happens, so the caller can rely on the callee's behavior only as far as it knows that code and whether the code behind the address can be replaced, and a target supplied by whoever invoked the caller, such as a token address passed as an argument, has to be treated as arbitrary code

what a message call carries and returns in EVM terminology: a sender, a recipient, a value, input data and an allowance of gas going in, and a success flag, return data and the unused part of the allowance coming back; and that a transaction's execution either begins with a message call or creates a contract, while code issues a message call for every further call, which is why what block explorers list as internal transactions are actions of code within a transaction, chiefly the message calls and contract creations it issues, not transactions

what a message call to an account without code does, built-in precompiled contracts aside: provided the caller can cover the value and the call depth bound has not been reached, it transfers the value and succeeds without running anything, so the same message is a payment or an invocation depending on what is at the recipient, and a caller that expects code there cannot take success as evidence that code ran

how a callee's failure is reported to its caller rather than imposed on it: the caller receives a failure flag and, when the callee reverted, the data it reverted with, the callee's changes are discarded, the unused allowance comes back when the callee reverts but is consumed when it halts exceptionally, such as by running out of gas, and the caller's execution continues until its own code decides; why language-level calls often propagate the failure automatically while low-level calls, such as Solidity's, leave the flag for the code to check

how a contract's code and initial state enter the system: on EVM-style platforms a creation transaction, or a call from an existing contract such as a factory, runs initialization code once, which sets the initial state and returns the code that will be stored, so the initialization code itself is not kept; and how platforms that separate uploading code from creating instances of it differ, letting many contracts share one stored program

how a new contract's address is determined and what follows from each scheme: derived from the creator and a per-creator counter, such as its account nonce, so it depends on how many transactions or creations the creator has made before, or from the creator, a chosen salt and the initialization code, so it can be known and used, for example funded, before the contract exists, while it fixes the code that will be stored only when that initialization code always produces the same code

what deployment fixes and what it leaves open: setup done during creation runs exactly once, as the creator's initialization code and arguments define it, while setup left to a separate initialization call afterward, as with code deployed behind a proxy, leaves a window, when that call is sent separately and does not restrict who may make it, in which another party can make that call first, and a contract can stay uninitialized or be misconfigured

what an execution environment exposes to running code beyond its input and storage, such as the immediate caller, the originating account, the value sent with the call, the contract's own address, block values and the remaining metered resources, and who sets each: the platform from the path of calls, the calling code for the value and resources it passes on, the transaction's sender through the transaction's fields, or, for block values, the protocol's rules and the block producer

what each context value can be trusted for: the immediate caller is set by the platform and cannot be chosen by the calling code, while the originating account names whoever signed or submitted the transaction, which every contract on the call path sees alike and which, where transactions are relayed or bundled, can be a relayer rather than the user; some block values are chosen or influenced by the block producer within bounds the protocol sets, so they are weak sources of fine-grained time and of randomness the producer cannot bias; and the remaining metered resources are what the caller chose to pass on, so code that branches on them can be steered by its caller

how what a callee sees changes along a chain of calls: the immediate caller and the value are set anew for each call, while the originating account stays fixed for the whole transaction, and so do block values where the whole chain of calls runs within one block, and a delegate-style call leaves the calling contract's caller, value and own address in place for the borrowed code, so a check that is sound in one call can mean something else in another

the phases a deployed contract can pass through, in use, changed, disabled and removed, and why which transitions exist is a design choice fixed at deployment, though a provided upgrade path can add transitions later and renouncing an authority can remove them: short of a change to the platform's own rules, a transition is possible only if the contract's code or the platform provides it, so a contract that provides none can only be used or abandoned; some transitions can be reversed, as when a paused contract resumes, and others cannot

how a contract whose code cannot change is still changed in effect: routing calls through indirection to replaceable logic keeps the contract's address and, where the state lives at that address or in storage the replaceable logic does not own, its state, while migrating to a new contract leaves the old one in place and callable unless it is disabled, and requires users, integrations and state to move to the new address

what disabling or removing a contract can and cannot achieve: disabling stops chosen interactions, through the contract's own code or, on some platforms, a mechanism the platform provides, often leaving withdrawals open, while removal, where a platform permits it, deletes its code, and the state held in its own account, from the current state but not from the chain's history, so on a chain whose history is public past transactions and states stay readable wherever nodes or archives keep history, and value sent to a removed contract's address afterward can be lost; some platforms have restricted removal

model.meaning: The data a smart contract keeps between its invocations: held for it by the platform, changed (under the platform's rules) only by code executed against it, and read by the contract's later invocations.

placements.contract-state: Single L2 placement, a leaf under Smart Contracts: the text must stand alone without the parent's synthesis, use no positional references, and stay platform-general, scoping each statement (account-tied storage, transparent chain, metered platform) and using EVM-style designs only as named examples.

contents: Persistent values the contract's code reads and writes across invocations: tracked balances, ownership and role records, configuration, counters, commitments. On EVM-style platforms held as the contract account's storage; on program/data-account designs (e.g. Solana) in separate accounts owned by the program. Storage layout, slots, account-state, global-state, persistent-storage: name only.

Pitfall: the account's native balance is account state but not the storage the code governs; on EVM it can grow without the contract's code running (value sent by another contract's self-destruct, fee-recipient or withdrawal credits). Keep claim 1 about the contract's stored data, not 'everything at its account'.

Pitfall: values fixed at deployment can live in the code rather than in storage (e.g. Solidity constants and immutables); 'must remember between invocations' concerns data set or changed after deployment.

One term, one sense: F1 State uses 'private state' for what a participant keeps for itself. Here 'private' is a language visibility keyword; write 'a variable marked private', never 'private state'. Contract state is shared state in F1's sense (named, not explained).
producedBy: Initial values at deployment (contract-deployment's territory: name only). After that, written by code executed against the state: the contract's own code, or code it borrows through a delegate-style call. Other contracts and users change it only by invoking the contract and having its code make the write.

Condition: on platforms that tie storage to the contract's account (on program/data-account designs the equivalent rule is that only the owning program may modify an account's data), and short of a change to the platform's own rules, such as a hard fork that alters state outside any contract's code. Do not write 'no one can ever' without that condition.
A write lasts only if the enclosing execution commits; reverted work leaves nothing (invocation endings are contract-execution's; transaction-reversion named only).
checkedBy: Full nodes executing the same transactions compute the same state, so the network checks that state follows from the code and the inputs, not that the code's logic does what its users intend. Encapsulation fixes the write path, not the correctness of writes.

What it leaves open (claim 1): the contract's own flawed logic (a missing check; reentrancy only named, as one class); authority the code grants (an owner, admin or upgrade role, which can then change data within that power; access-control named only); code borrowed through a delegate-style call, which writes with the contract's full power because the boundary is the account, not the code that runs. The EVM record already explains delegate call and slot-level trust: reference, do not restate.
lifetime: Persistent state outlives each committed invocation and is what later invocations read; it lasts until overwritten or deleted, or until the contract is removed where a platform permits removal (contract-lifecycle: name only). On platforms that charge rent for stored data or give it a lifetime, it can also leave the live state while the contract still exists when that lifetime lapses without being extended (deleted or set aside until restored, by platform; why storage is charged is storage-costs': name only). Overwriting, deleting or otherwise removing does not erase past values from history wherever history is kept (ties to claim 2).

Working data lasts one invocation (e.g. EVM memory and local values, discarded when the call frame ends; not shared between two invocations of the same contract, including a reentrant one); some platforms add a space that lasts one transaction and is shared by its invocations (EVM transient storage, EIP-1153). It is still working data: do not call it persistent, and do not say working data in general lasts a transaction.

Consequence: whatever a later invocation must know (a balance, a lock or flag that spans transactions, a commitment, a recorded deadline) has to be in persistent state, or be supplied again by the caller and checked against something persistent such as a stored hash. On metered platforms writing persistent state is often among the costliest operations; why and how much is storage-costs' (name only; keep 'often').

Code and data persist independently: on EVM an account's code is fixed at deployment while its storage keeps changing; logic is replaced either through indirection (the proxy keeps the state and borrows replaceable logic; proxy-patterns named only) or, on platforms that allow it, by replacing the code at the same account (e.g. upgradeable Solana programs). Either way existing data stays and the new code must read it as the old code wrote it: stored values carry no type, so meaning comes from the code's layout (storage-layout named only). New code also inherits whatever the old code got wrong: fixing a bug does not repair state the bug already wrote.

Replacing a contract with a new one at a new address leaves the state at the old account; moving it is an explicit migration (state-migrations named only), and the old contract's fate is contract-lifecycle's.
invariants: On account-tied platforms, a contract account's storage changes only through code executed against that account (own or borrowed), with the platform-rules condition. The EVM record states this for the EVM: reference it; contract-state's angle is what the invariant does and does not protect.

No corresponding invariant on reads: on a transparent chain anything in the state that full nodes hold can be read off-chain whatever its language visibility; visibility keywords restrict only what code can reach through the language (e.g. Solidity private: no getter, no access from derived contracts).
variants: Read access by other contracts differs by platform (hence 'many platforms' in claim 2): on EVM no instruction reads another account's storage, so other contracts read only what its code exposes; on program/data-account designs any program can read an account passed to it. Pitfall: this restricts direct access, not knowledge; anyone who reads the value off-chain can pass it to any contract as input, so it gives no secrecy.

Claim 2's 'public' holds on transparent chains. Platforms that encrypt state or execute privately (execution-privacy, privacy: named only) are outside it; scope the statement rather than say 'all contract state is public'.

Full nodes hold the current state and may prune older states; archive nodes keep past states, and anyone can recompute any past state by replaying the public transactions from the start. Do not say every node stores all past state.
tradeoffs: Keeping a secret (claim 2): off-chain means never in storage and never in any transaction's input or event, since inputs and logs are public too; encrypted means the ciphertext is public and is safe only while the key stays off-chain and the encryption holds, and a contract on a transparent chain cannot decrypt it without exposing the key; a hash commitment hides the value only if it cannot be guessed (add enough randomness, e.g. a salt) and the reveal is public when it comes (commit-reveal named only).
Overwriting, deleting or otherwise removing a value later does not make it secret again: once written or sent in a transaction it stays recoverable wherever the chain's history is kept.

Argument and conditions; no order, recurrence, persistent modes or shared dimensions.

model.meaning: One run of a contract's code from the moment an invocation enters it to the moment it returns or fails: how the code selects what to run from the input, what it can compute over while running, and what its ending decides for that run.

This concept adds the unit those sentences assume: one invocation, how it is entered and dispatched, the full set of channels its computation can draw on (the parent names only the context), that code runs only when invoked and what that does to time-based rules, and what an invocation's ending decides for that invocation. Domain premise: 'Local contract execution can therefore become part of a much larger execution graph' - this record stays on the local run.

placements.contract-execution: Single placement, a leaf under Smart Contracts in Computation & Execution. Platform-general framing holds there; when an EVM example is used (selector dispatch, revert data), mark it as one platform's way and pair it with a contrast where the claim is general. No positional references.

sequence: Entry and dispatch (claim 1). Two families, plus a hybrid the author must not erase: (a) code-level dispatch, as on the EVM: the VM has no notion of functions; the compiler (Solidity, Vyper) emits a dispatcher that matches the first 4 bytes of the input against the selectors of the contract's externally callable functions (public and external functions, including generated getters; internal and private functions have no selector and cannot be reached through the input; a selector is the first 4 bytes of the Keccak-256 hash of the canonical signature: name plus parameter types), then decodes the arguments from the rest; (b) runtime dispatch by name, as on NEAR, where the runtime calls the exported WASM function the call names; (c) hybrids: Solana programs and CosmWasm contracts have fixed entry points the runtime calls, and the program's own code then dispatches on the instruction or message data. So do not say every non-EVM or every WASM platform calls the target function by name; 'on others' is right, 'on WASM platforms' is not.

Default path, Solidity terms for accuracy: receive runs on empty input (a plain value transfer); fallback runs when no selector matches, or on empty input when there is no receive; with neither defined, such a call reverts. Vyper has a single default function. 'If the contract defines one' is the condition: without it, unmatched input fails.
Running (claim 2): the code computes over its channels only; it cannot fetch anything during the run.

Ending (claim 4): normal return (with output, or none), explicit revert (with error data), or a failure the code did not choose (resource exhaustion, an invalid operation). See failures and invariants for the conditions.
actors: The invoker: a transaction's sender at the top level, or another contract's code for a nested invocation. Who supplies the input decides how far it can be trusted: input is chosen by the caller and must be treated as adversarial.
The runtime/VM: delivers input and environment values, runs the code, enforces limits (metering, gas and resource-limits named only).
Compiler: generates the dispatcher and argument decoding on code-level-dispatch platforms; the dispatch logic is part of the deployed code, not the VM.
Parties outside the chain who must act for the contract: whoever supplies off-chain facts (oracle-problem named only) and whoever invokes at a due time (keepers named only).
inputs: Channels (claim 2): the contract's own state; the call's input; what the execution environment supplies (caller, value, own address, block values, remaining metered resources - execution-context owns what each is and what it can be trusted for: name it, do not list trust properties); what the calls it makes return (contract-calls owns what a caller can assume about a callee).

Accuracy limits on 'namely': on the EVM, code can also query some facts about other accounts without calling them (balance, code size and code hash) and read its own code's embedded constants; some platforms add per-transaction storage (EVM transient storage). Fold these into 'own state' and 'environment' or hedge the list; do not present four channels as exhaustive in a way these contradict. On Solana a program reads only accounts the transaction passed in, which fits 'arrives through the input'.

Why nothing else can enter: every node re-runs the code and must reach the same result, so code cannot read local, external or time-varying sources (deterministic-execution named, not explained). An off-chain fact (a price) has to be written into chain state by some party's transaction, or passed in the input, possibly with a signature the code verifies. A verified signature establishes who vouched for the value, not that it is true. Designs that let code request external data (e.g. the Internet Computer's HTTPS outcalls) still deliver it through a protocol channel whose suppliers are trusted; the principle holds, do not claim external data is impossible on every platform.

Conclusion the record must keep with its condition: the contract's conclusions are as reliable as the parties behind the channels they depend on; the code cannot tell a true supplied value from a false one unless it can check it against something it already trusts.
outputs: On return: output data to the invoker, and the invocation's state changes (including those of calls it made that succeeded) kept, provisionally wherever an enclosing execution can still fail (see assumptions); nothing encloses the top-level invocation, and in designs that commit each deferred execution on its own, such as NEAR's receipts, a finished invocation's changes are committed.

On failure: the invocation's changes discarded; an explicit revert hands back error data; a failure the code did not choose generally hands back none (on the EVM an exceptional halt returns empty data). What the caller receives as a flag and what happens to the resource allowance are message-calls' and transaction-reversion's: name, do not explain.
What an ending does not output: any decision about the caller's own changes. The invoker propagates or handles the failure (contract-calls owns this; name only).
assumptions: Claim 3's premise holds on platforms where code runs only when a transaction or another contract invokes it (Ethereum and most account-based chains). Some platforms schedule runs themselves (Internet Computer canister timers, chain-level scheduled hooks on some Cosmos SDK chains, deferred calls on some newer chains); there the scheduled run is a protocol-initiated invocation and no external caller is needed. Hedge 'a contract runs only inside invocations' and 'needs an external caller' with this condition.

Claim 4's 'settles nothing beyond the invocation, since the enclosing execution can still fail' holds where the invocation is nested in a larger synchronous execution (a call inside a call or transaction). After the top-level invocation of an EVM transaction returns, nothing in the transaction can undo it. In designs that commit each deferred execution on its own, such as NEAR's receipts, an invocation's changes are committed when it finishes, and a later failure elsewhere does not undo them; contract-calls owns async calls: name only.

Code runs only inside invocations, but not everything in a contract's account changes only then: on the EVM value can be forced into a contract's balance without running its code (as the beneficiary of a self-destruct, or as a fee or withdrawal recipient). Do not write that nothing about a contract changes without an invocation.
failures: Dispatch mismatch (claim 1): caller and callee must share the encoding (selector scheme and argument layout). A wrong or absent selector reaches the default path if one exists, otherwise fails; short arguments or values invalid for their types make Solidity's decoder revert, but a mismatch need not fail: under a format that does not describe itself (such as Borsh) mis-encoded bytes can still parse and run the function with values the caller did not mean, so the default path is one place, not the only one, where a mismatch passes unnoticed. A permissive default path that accepts any input and does not revert makes a call to a missing function succeed with no effect - documented case: WETH's fallback deposits, so a call to a permit function WETH does not have succeeded silently, and a bridge (Multichain, 2022) that relied on permit reverting was drained. If used, state the condition (default path accepts input and does not revert) and keep the angle on what the callee runs; what the caller may rely on is contract-calls'.

Selector collisions: selectors are 4 bytes, so different signatures can share one; compilers reject a collision within one contract. Do not say selectors are unique; do not explain proxy selector clashes (proxy-patterns, not this concept).
Trusting a channel's supplier (claim 2): caller-chosen input, a returned value from untrusted code, or a pushed price taken as fact.

Time rules (claim 3): nothing happens at a deadline itself. Code that compares the current block's time to the deadline at each invocation enforces it correctly whenever it next runs, but anything that should happen at the deadline (a payout, a liquidation, a status change) waits for someone to invoke; code that stores a status flag instead of computing it from time acts on a stale flag until updated. Time is read from block values when the code runs (producer-influenced: execution-context's, name only). An action due at a time depends on someone paying to invoke it; if no one does, it does not happen. Do not say the contract 'misses' a deadline or has no notion of time.

Ending (claim 4): discarded changes on revert; a nested success later undone by an enclosing failure. Do not enumerate revert triggers, their costs, or why fees and nonce updates survive (transaction-reversion); do not explain journaling, checkpoints or per-call narrowing of the all-or-nothing unit (transaction-atomicity); do not explain frames or call kinds (evm).
fields.variants: Dispatch families: compiler-generated dispatch in the code (EVM selectors), runtime call of an exported entry by name (NEAR), fixed runtime entry points with dispatch in the code (Solana, CosmWasm). Two or three, one attribute each: prose, not a structure.
fields.tradeoffs: Time-dependent rules: lazy evaluation at the next invocation costs nothing until then but leaves deadline-driven effects undone until someone acts; paying callers to invoke on time (keepers named only) makes the effect timely but depends on someone being paid and willing, so liveness rests on them. One clause each; no keeper mechanics.
fields.invariants: Within one invocation the code's results depend only on its channels; its ending decides, for the invocation itself, whether its changes stand (a return keeps them provisionally wherever an enclosing execution can still fail), and nothing above it. Both carry their conditions (see assumptions).

design.relationship: Four claims about one unit of execution: how it is entered (a dispatch with platform variants and a shared-encoding argument), what it computes over (an argument from replicated re-execution to trust in suppliers), why code runs only when invoked (a consequence for time-based rules, with a trade-off), and how it ends (two or three outcomes with conditional provisional effect). The relationships are causal and conditional: 'because', 'only if', 'unless', 'where nested'.
design.whyProse: The only ordered element, enter, run, end, is a three-step linear sequence that a sentence states; a flow would add nothing and would invite restating EVM frame structure. Dispatch has two or three variants with one attribute each, which representation-design says are prose or a sentence, not a comparison. The endings are not persistent states with returns, so no state model; there is no recurring loop for a cycle. 'Returned' versus 'settled' is a single conflation stated in a clause with its condition; a distinction block would strip the condition (nested synchronous execution) that makes it true. Each claim is an argument whose conditions carry the meaning, which paragraphs keep and structures drop.
design.level: The parent states that code is the authority, that calls hand over control and that context informs a contract, assuming an invocation as the unit; the mechanics of that unit (entry, inputs, time, ending) belong to this concept. Transaction-level processing is transaction-execution's; machine-level frames and call kinds are evm's; this concept sits between them at one run of one contract's code.
design.territory: Names, without explaining: execution-context (what each context value is and its trust), contract-calls (caller's assumptions, failure propagation, async), message-calls (flag, return data, allowance), contract-state (persistent vs working data), evm and wasm (frames, call kinds, VM constraints), transaction-execution (the per-transaction envelope), transaction-reversion (revert triggers, costs, what survives, revert data use), transaction-atomicity (what the unit covers, journaling, per-call narrowing), deterministic-execution, oracle-problem, keepers, metering, gas, resource-limits. Claim 4 stays on the single invocation: what its own ending decides for its own changes and what it hands back, with the provisional status named and its mechanism left to transaction-atomicity.
design.placements: One leaf placement under Smart Contracts; the platform-general framing with EVM examples marked as examples holds there.

model.meaning: A contract call is one contract invoking code at another address, either synchronously within the same execution or asynchronously as a message executed later, with the timing deciding when the caller can use the result and shaping whether and how a failure reaches it, and the code at the target, not the caller's expectation, deciding what happens.

parents.smart-contracts: Parent states that contracts call one another, that a call hands control to code the caller does not control, that the callee can fail, consume resources or call back, and that a caller must be correct for whatever called code might do. Do not restate any of that. Adds: the two timing models across platforms (sync call-and-return vs async message) and what each means for using the result and for stale state; how failure crosses the boundary in each (platform-dependent for sync; committed-before-known for async); and what naming a target actually binds (address + expected interface vs the code there, its replaceability, caller-supplied targets).

claims: how one contract invokes another across platforms: synchronously, with the caller suspended until the callee returns within the same execution and the result usable at once, or asynchronously, with a message delivered and executed later, possibly in another block, shard or chain, while the caller continues, so the caller cannot use the result in the same step and the state it acted on may have changed by the time a reply arrives

how failure crosses a call boundary: in a synchronous call, on platforms that let the caller observe the failure, the caller either propagates the callee's failure, so its own work is undone with it, or handles the failure and continues with its own changes kept; in an asynchronous design the caller's changes may already be committed before the failure is known, so the failure arrives, if the design reports it at all, as a later reply or returned message and the caller has to reverse its own effects with explicit compensating steps

what a call target binds and what it does not: a caller names an address and an expected interface, but the code at that address decides what happens, so the caller can rely on the callee's behavior only as far as it knows that code and whether the code behind the address can be replaced, and a target supplied by whoever invoked the caller, such as a token address passed as an argument, has to be treated as arbitrary code

placements.contract-calls: Single L2 placement under Smart Contracts (Computation & Execution). Exposition is platform-general, so it holds without the parent; it must not lean on EVM-only mechanics, which evm and message-calls own.

sequence: Sync: caller issues call, its execution is suspended, callee runs (and may make nested calls) within the same execution, on success returns a result and the caller resumes with it usable at once; on failure, depending on the platform, the caller resumes and can respond (EVM) or the whole transaction aborts and the caller never resumes (Solana cross-program invocations, Move aborts). Examples that fit the synchronous timing and success path: EVM calls, Solana cross-program invocations, Move cross-module calls.

Async: caller emits a message and its own execution goes on (typically to completion) without the callee's result; the message is executed later: after the caller returns but in the same transaction on some designs, in a later block on others (e.g. NEAR receipts), on another shard or chain on others (cross-chain-calls: name only). A reply, if any, is a further message the caller handles in a separate later invocation.

Some platforms mix both (e.g. synchronous read-only queries with asynchronous state-changing messages, or synchronous calls on one chain and asynchronous messages across chains). Do not present sync/async as an exhaustive per-platform binary.
actors: Caller contract: chooses target, arguments, and (sync, on platforms that report the failure to it) what to do with a failure.
Callee: whatever code is at the target address; it decides the behavior.
Platform runtime: delivers the call or message and defines whether a failure can be caught.
Whoever invoked the caller: may supply the target (e.g. a token address passed as an argument), so may choose the code that runs.
Whoever can replace the code behind an address (name proxy-patterns only; do not explain upgrade mechanics or restate the parent's point about upgrade authority).
fields.inputs: Keep general: a target address, the function or entry point and arguments per an expected interface, and on many platforms value or a resource allowance. Do NOT list the EVM message-call fields (sender, recipient, value, input data, gas): message-calls owns that list.
fields.outputs: Sync: a result returned to the caller in the same execution; a failure is returned to the caller only on platforms that let it observe one (e.g. EVM), elsewhere it aborts the whole transaction. Async: nothing in the same step; possibly a later reply or returned message, only if the design or the caller arranges one (e.g. a callback attached by the caller, a bounced message). Pitfall: do not say a failure always comes back in async designs; on some the caller never learns of it unless it asked for a reply.
assumptions: The caller's expected interface is an expectation, not a guarantee: on many platforms nothing checks at call time that the target implements it, and even where linking checks signatures (e.g. Move) the callee's code still decides behavior. What happens on an input mismatch is contract-execution's (name only).

Relying on the callee's behavior needs knowledge of the code actually at that address AND of whether, and by whom, it can be replaced. Avoid 'cannot change' absolutes: replaceability depends on platform and the contract's design.

A target supplied by an untrusted invoker must be treated as arbitrary code: it can conform to the interface in form while doing anything, e.g. a fake token reporting a successful transfer that moved nothing, failing, or calling back (reentrancy: name only).

Sync failure handling is platform-dependent: on the EVM the caller observes a failure and may propagate it or continue; on others a failed callee aborts the whole transaction and the caller cannot handle it (Solana cross-program invocations; Move aborts). Condition the either/or claim accordingly.
failures: Sync, propagate: the caller fails too, so its own changes are undone with the callee's. Do not explain frame-level undo (evm) or transaction-level reversion (transaction-reversion, transaction-atomicity: name only).

Sync, handle: the caller continues with its own changes kept, for the time being: an enclosing execution can still fail (contract-execution owns that; name only). Silently ignoring a failure is unchecked-external-calls (name only). Do not explain the EVM success flag, return data, gas refund on revert, or language vs low-level call behavior: message-calls owns them.

Async: the caller's changes may already be committed when the callee fails (not on designs that dispatch messages within the same transaction and revert it on failure), so the failure can only arrive later, if reported, and undoing the caller's effects takes explicit compensating steps (compensating-actions: name only; do not explain sagas or compensation design).

Async staleness: between sending and any reply, other transactions can change the state the caller checked and the callee's state, so the reply may describe a world that no longer holds. Do not develop composability consequences (synchronous-composability, asynchronous-composability, composability: name only).
fields.variants: Synchronous call-and-return vs asynchronous message passing, plus hybrids. Two alternatives, each a causal chain with conditions; not a catalog.
fields.tradeoffs: Sync: result usable at once and the caller can make its own work depend on the callee's success, but the callee runs mid-execution and both must run in one execution environment. Async: lets calls cross shards or chains, which designs placing contracts there commonly rely on, but gives up the immediate result and the shared undo. Pitfall: do not claim cross-shard calls must be async; some designs coordinate synchronously.
fields.invariants: Sync, on platforms that execute transactions with serial-equivalent results: while the call is in progress, the state the caller read changes only through what the callee and its nested calls do. Async: no such guarantee; other transactions may run between send and reply.

design.relationship: Two timing models whose differences are causal chains (when the callee runs -> whether the result is usable -> how failure crosses and whether the caller's work can be undone with it), plus an argument about what naming a target binds.
design.whyProse: Each claim is an argument whose truth rests on its conditions: which platforms let a caller catch a failure, whether an async design reports failure at all, whether the caller's changes are committed yet, whether code behind an address can be replaced and by whom. A comparison would set two alternatives on shared dimensions but compress those conditions into cells, and two alternatives are guidance's case for prose, not a two-row table; a failure-path flow would draw a clean branch where the sync branch is a platform property, not a caller's choice everywhere. Claim 3 has no shape of its own.
design.level: Belongs here, not at Smart Contracts (which states only that calls hand control to uncontrolled code and that callers must be robust to it) nor at Message Calls (the EVM unit and its failure report) nor at EVM (frames, depth bound, call kinds): the platform-general timing models, failure crossing and target binding are this concept's own.
design.territory: Draws no sibling's or reserved relationship: EVM frames, depth and call kinds stay with evm; message-call fields, the failure flag and gas return stay with message-calls; what code sees (caller, origin) stays with execution-context; how one invocation ends and that a nested success settles nothing stays with contract-execution; reentrancy, unchecked-external-calls, composability variants, cross-chain-calls, compensating-actions, transaction-atomicity, transaction-reversion, atomicity-guarantees and proxy-patterns are named only where a claim reaches them.
design.placements: One placement (Smart Contracts / Contract Calls); the prose is platform-general and self-standing, so it reads correctly there without depending on the parent's sentences.

model.meaning: In EVM terminology, the unit by which a transaction or running code addresses an account: it carries a sender, recipient, value, input data and a gas allowance, and returns a success flag, return data and unused gas; whether code runs depends on what is at the recipient.

parents.smart-contracts: Parent says contracts call one another, that a call hands control to code the caller does not control and that the callee can fail. Premises: do not restate. Adds the EVM unit underneath: what goes in and comes back, that the same message is a payment or an invocation by what sits at the recipient (the domain sentence's 'may execute contract code'), and what exactly the caller is handed when the callee fails.

claims: what a message call carries and returns in EVM terminology: a sender, a recipient, a value, input data and an allowance of gas going in, and a success flag, return data and the unused part of the allowance coming back; and that a transaction's execution either begins with a message call or creates a contract, while code issues a message call for every further call, which is why what block explorers list as internal transactions are actions of code within a transaction, chiefly the message calls and contract creations it issues, not transactions

what a message call to an account without code does, built-in precompiled contracts aside: provided the caller can cover the value and the call depth bound has not been reached, it transfers the value and succeeds without running anything, so the same message is a payment or an invocation depending on what is at the recipient, and a caller that expects code there cannot take success as evidence that code ran

how a callee's failure is reported to its caller rather than imposed on it: the caller receives a failure flag and, when the callee reverted, the data it reverted with, the callee's changes are discarded, the unused allowance comes back when the callee reverts but is consumed when it halts exceptionally, such as by running out of gas, and the caller's execution continues until its own code decides; why language-level calls often propagate the failure automatically while low-level calls, such as Solidity's, leave the flag for the code to check

placements.message-calls: Single placement, under smart-contracts. Write EVM-specific throughout and say so (the claims are 'in EVM terminology'); EVM-compatible chains share the model, but do not generalize to other platforms (contract-calls owns the platform-general view).

inputs: Sender (ordinary call): the immediate caller, i.e. the transaction's sender for the top-level call, the calling contract's address for a code-issued call; value moves from sender to recipient. Delegate-style calls are the exception: they keep a different sender and value in place and move no value. What they keep is execution-context's and evm's: name at most.

Recipient address; value (may be zero; static and delegate-style calls move no value: name only, call kinds are evm's); input data (empty for a plain payment; its encoding and dispatch are contract-execution's); gas allowance (top level: what the transaction leaves after its intrinsic cost; code-issued: what the caller passes, which the EVM caps; gas and metering are named, not explained).

Pitfall: the formal definition carries more parameters (originator, gas price, depth, static flag). Present these five as what the message carries from the caller's side, not as an exhaustive or exact list.
outputs: Success flag (for a code-issued call, a 1 or 0 the caller's code receives); return data (what the callee returned, or the data it reverted with; empty after an exceptional halt, after a call that ran nothing, and after a call rejected before running); unused allowance back to the caller.
Unused gas does not always come back: after an exceptional halt the callee's whole allowance is consumed. Do not state 'the unused part comes back' unconditionally.
Top-level call: the outcome reaches the transaction (receipt status, leftover gas refunded to the sender, fees still paid). That is transaction-execution's and transaction-reversion's: name only.
sequence: Origin: a transaction with a recipient starts its execution with a message call; a transaction without one creates a contract instead. Every further call is issued by running code (the call instructions); creations by code are contract creations, not message calls.

Before anything runs, the call can be rejected: depth bound reached, or the caller's balance cannot cover the value. Then it fails without running, nothing changes and the allowance returns. Separate case: a caller that cannot pay the call's own cost halts itself; that is not a failure reported to it.

In an ordinary call, value moves to the recipient (delegate-style calls move none). Then by what is there: code runs (in a frame: evm's, name only); a precompiled contract runs its built-in function; no code means nothing runs and the call succeeds.

Outcome returns to the caller: flag, return data, unused gas. On failure the callee's changes, including the value transfer and its own sub-calls' effects, are discarded; the caller's are not touched and its code continues and decides (handle, ignore, or revert itself and so pass failure upward). The undo structure itself is evm's: say only what the caller sees.

Internal transactions: explorers reconstruct them by tracing execution; they are not in the block as transactions, are not signed, and have no fee or receipt of their own. Pitfall: explorers differ in what they list (some show only value-carrying calls, and value moved by self-destruct also appears), so do not say every listed entry is a message call or that every message call is listed.
actors: Caller: an externally submitted transaction (top level) or a running contract (code-issued). Externally-owned and contract accounts are named only.
Recipient: decides by what it holds whether the message is a payment or an invocation; the caller does not choose this, it only names an address.
Language and compiler: decide whether a failure flag is checked or propagated for the programmer (claim 3).
assumptions: Codeless is not the same as 'user account': since Pectra (May 2025, EIP-7702) a user account can carry a delegation designator, and calling it runs the delegated code; an address whose contract is not yet deployed, or a contract still running its own construction, has no code at that moment. Use 'account without code', as the claim does.

Revert versus exceptional halt: REVERT (Byzantium, 2017) lets code stop, undo and return data while handing back unused gas; exceptional halts (out of gas, invalid instruction, a state change attempted under a static call, among others) consume the whole allowance and return no data. Do not invent a rationale such as 'penalty'.

Language-level versus low-level (claim 3): Solidity's high-level external calls revert when the callee fails, passing the callee's revert data upward, unless wrapped in try/catch; they also check that the target has code (since 0.8.10 skipped when return data is expected, where decoding empty data fails instead). Solidity's low-level call, delegatecall, staticcall and send return the flag and check no code; transfer reverts on failure. Vyper's raw_call reverts by default and returns the flag only when told not to revert. So 'often' for language-level; do not write that every low-level call leaves the flag.
failures: Success that means nothing ran: a value or data call to a wrong, undeployed or codeless address succeeds with empty return data; a low-level caller that treats the flag as proof of execution is misled (claim 2). A high-level call that expects return data fails instead, because empty data cannot be decoded.
Failure flag ignored: the caller carries on as if the callee acted. This is unchecked-external-calls' bug class: name only, do not explain exploitation.
Flag alone does not say why: rejected before running, reverted, and halted all read as failure; return data and gas consumption differ (see the design's comparison).
Do not explain reentrancy, the depth bound or why deep nesting runs out of gas first: evm and the parent cover these.
variants: By what is at the recipient: code (invocation), no code (payment, nothing runs), precompiled contract (built-in function, not EVM code; its own failure rules, name only). The message is the same in each; only the recipient differs.

design.relationship: One message, several outcomes the caller must tell apart: the success flag collapses outcomes that differ in what they mean (code ran versus nothing ran; reverted versus halted versus rejected before running), and only the other returned items (return data, unused gas, whether the callee's changes stand) distinguish them.

structures.purpose: Outcomes of a message call (callee code returns normally; no code at the recipient; callee reverts; callee halts exceptionally, such as out of gas; rejected before running, because the value is not covered or the depth bound is reached) read across what the caller gets back: success flag, return data, the callee's changes including the value, unused allowance.
structures.whyNotProse: The two claims turn on reading across rows: normal return and no-code success share a flag but differ in whether anything ran (claim 2), and revert and exceptional halt share a flag and discarded changes but differ in return data and gas (claim 3). Prose spreads these five-by-four values across many sentences and buries which pairs look alike to the caller.

design.division: Prose explains what the message carries and where calls come from (transaction or code; why internal transactions are not transactions), why the same message is a payment or an invocation and what success therefore does not show, that the caller's code continues and decides after a failure, and why language-level calls often propagate failure while Solidity-style low-level calls hand back the flag. The comparison shows only the per-outcome values; prose must not re-list them row by row, and the table carries no reasons.
design.level: The outcomes are those of the EVM's message-call unit, which this concept owns; the parent speaks of calls generally, evm owns frames, depth and call kinds rather than what a call returns, and contract-calls owns the platform-general propagate-or-handle choice, not the EVM's returned values.
design.territory: The table compares outcomes of one ordinary message call, not kinds of call (evm's), not synchronous versus asynchronous calling (contract-calls'), and not what a failed transaction keeps (transaction-reversion's). The gas column states only what the claims state (returned or consumed), naming gas and metering without explaining pricing or the cap on what a caller can pass. Ignoring the flag is named as unchecked-external-calls; the undo of nested frames is named as evm's.
design.placements: One placement under smart-contracts; the exposition is explicitly EVM-scoped, so it holds there without depending on the parent's wording.

model.meaning: Contract deployment (one contract's creation, not a protocol launch): how a smart contract's code and initial state enter a platform, how its address is set, and what creation fixes versus leaves to later calls.

parents.smart-contracts: Parent states as premise that deployment fixes the code and that on many platforms deployed code cannot be changed; do not restate or argue it. Adds: the creation mechanism (init code run once, returned code stored; or upload-then-instantiate), address determination and its consequences, and the split between setup the platform runs once at creation and setup left to a later call that only the contract's own code guards. Parent's upgradeability and authority points belong to contract-lifecycle / proxy-patterns; name only.

claims: how a contract's code and initial state enter the system: on EVM-style platforms a creation transaction, or a call from an existing contract such as a factory, runs initialization code once, which sets the initial state and returns the code that will be stored, so the initialization code itself is not kept; and how platforms that separate uploading code from creating instances of it differ, letting many contracts share one stored program

how a new contract's address is determined and what follows from each scheme: derived from the creator and a per-creator counter, such as its account nonce, so it depends on how many transactions or creations the creator has made before, or from the creator, a chosen salt and the initialization code, so it can be known and used, for example funded, before the contract exists, while it fixes the code that will be stored only when that initialization code always produces the same code

what deployment fixes and what it leaves open: setup done during creation runs exactly once, as the creator's initialization code and arguments define it, while setup left to a separate initialization call afterward, as with code deployed behind a proxy, leaves a window, when that call is sent separately and does not restrict who may make it, in which another party can make that call first, and a contract can stay uninitialized or be misconfigured

placements.contract-deployment: Only placement (Computation & Execution / Smart Contracts, label 'Deployment'). Hazard: the label also names protocol launch (protocol-deployment, deployment-launch); open on a contract's creation so the label cannot be read as launch. Nothing here depends on wording placed elsewhere.

sequence: EVM-style, one step: a creation transaction (no recipient; data = init code, with constructor arguments appended by tooling) or a create instruction issued by running code, e.g. a factory contract (name factory-patterns only).
Address is determined before init code runs (see variants).

Init code runs once in the new account's context: it can write initial state and receive value; it returns bytes, and those bytes become the stored code. Init code itself is not stored as the account's code (pitfall: it stays readable in chain history as the creation transaction's input when deployed by transaction, so say 'not kept as the contract's code', not 'erased').

Separate-upload platforms (e.g. CosmWasm: store code -> code id; instantiate with code id + init message -> new address with its own state; the instance's init entry point runs once at instantiation). Initial state is set at instantiation, not upload; many instances run one stored program. Avoid Solana as an instance example: its programs serve separate data accounts and do not form per-instance contracts in the same sense; leave it out or frame it precisely.
Stop at the stored code and initial state; what happens to the contract afterward is contract-lifecycle's.
actors: Creator: an externally owned account sending a creation transaction, or running code executing a create instruction. On Ethereum the salt-based scheme exists only as an instruction, so salt-based deployment is issued by running code (often a shared deterministic-deployment factory).
Initializer: whoever makes a post-creation initialization call; under a separate-initializer design it is whoever calls first unless code restricts it.
Platform: computes the address, runs init code, stores the returned code, rejects collisions and failed creations.
fields.inputs: Creator address; per-creator counter (on Ethereum the account nonce: for an externally owned account it counts every transaction sent, not only deployments; for a contract it counts its creations, starting at 1); for the salt scheme, a salt chosen by the creator and the hash of the full init code (including constructor arguments, so different arguments give a different address); value sent; for split platforms, the code id and instantiation message.
fields.outputs: A new account at the determined address holding the code the init code returned and whatever state it wrote, plus any value sent. On failure (init code reverts, runs out of gas, returns code over the platform's size limit or otherwise rejected) no contract exists; on Ethereum the creator's counter still advances, unless the enclosing execution is itself reverted (a failed creation transaction from an externally owned account still uses its nonce).
assumptions: Counter scheme: an address can be computed in advance only by knowing the counter value at the time of creation; any other transaction or creation by the same creator first changes it. Do not say counter addresses cannot be predicted.

Salt scheme: address is independent of the creator's history, so it can be computed and used (e.g. sent value) before creation. Pre-funding works on Ethereum because a balance alone does not count as a collision; the value is retrievable only if code that can move it is later deployed there.

The salt-scheme address commits to the hash of the init code, not to the stored code. It pins the stored code only when that init code always returns the same code; init code that builds or copies its returned code from mutable external state can place different code at the same address in different circumstances. Do not develop metamorphic redeployment; if mentioned, Ethereum restricted the removal it relied on in 2024 (EIP-6780), and removal belongs to contract-lifecycle.

Once-only at creation is enforced by the platform: init code runs within that one creation and cannot be invoked again. A separate initialization function runs once only if the contract's own code enforces it (e.g. an initialized flag).

The window after deployment exists when the initialization call is a separate transaction and the function lets whoever calls first set it up; deploying and initializing in one transaction (e.g. a factory or proxy constructor that makes the call during creation) leaves no window. State the condition; do not write 'leaves a window' unconditionally.
failures: Creation fails: init code reverts or exhausts gas, returned code exceeds the size limit, or the address is occupied (on Ethereum, for example, existing code or a nonzero nonce); no contract results.
Initialization taken first by another party when a separate unrestricted initializer is called in a later transaction (name front-running; do not explain transaction ordering).

Contract left uninitialized, including a logic contract behind a proxy whose own initializer was never called; or initialized with wrong parameters, which, with code that cannot change, may be permanent. Optional example only if exact: the 2017 Parity multisig library, a shared library the wallets used through delegate calls, was left uninitialized; a user called its initialization function, became owner and destroyed it, freezing the wallets that depended on it. Otherwise omit.
Pitfall: security guidance (initializer guards, deployment scripts, verification) is deployment-security; name only.
variants: Address schemes: counter-based (creator + counter; depends on how many transactions or creations the creator made before) vs salt-based (creator + salt + init-code hash; reproducible on chains that derive these addresses the same way, known before creation). Differ chiefly on one axis, what the address depends on; consequences are conditional.

Deployment models: single-step creation (EVM: each contract carries its own stored code) vs separate upload and instantiation (many instances share one stored program). Do not claim EVM clients physically duplicate identical code; say each account has its own code. EVM code sharing via clones or proxies is factory-patterns / proxy-patterns, name only.
invariants: Init code runs at most once per created contract, and only during its creation.
What is stored is what the init code returned, fixed at creation; whether it can later change is the parent's premise and contract-lifecycle's subject.
Constructor-time values baked into stored code are fixed with it (name immutability only).
tradeoffs: Setup in creation: platform-enforced once-only and no window, but unavailable for the proxy's storage where code is reused through a proxy, because a logic contract's creation writes its own state, not the proxy's (one clause; do not explain delegation).
Salt scheme: predictability and cross-context reproducibility (on chains that derive these addresses the same way) vs commitment to exact init code and arguments, and to the creator's address.

design.relationship: A short creation process whose meaning lies in conditional consequences: what an address depends on decides when it can be known in advance and what it commits to; where setup runs decides whether once-only is enforced by the platform or only by the contract's code.
design.whyProse: The creation sequence is linear and four steps long, so a flow adds no order or branch prose does not state in a sentence. The two address schemes differ on one axis (what the address depends on), a variant pair rather than a comparison across shared dimensions, and their consequences hold only under conditions (counter known at creation; init code deterministic) that a table cell would drop. Single-step vs upload-then-instantiate is two models better explained in a paragraph each. Init code vs stored code is a point one sentence settles, not a conflation needing a distinction block. Setup-at-creation vs separate initializer is conditional reasoning (same transaction or not, guarded or not), which paragraphs carry and structures would flatten.
design.level: The parent states only the premise that deployment fixes code; the mechanics of creation, address determination and initialization timing are specific to this concept. What follows creation (phases, changes, removal) is contract-lifecycle's, so the account of creation stops at the stored code and initial state.
design.territory: Explains only the three claims. Names without explaining: factory-patterns (a factory as one kind of creator), proxy-patterns (only as the case that needs a separate initializer), front-running (a call made first), deployment-security, account-nonces (only as 'a per-creator counter'), addresses, contract-accounts, contract-state (initial state as an output, not storage layout), immutability, evm, contract-lifecycle. Leaves to message-calls the classification of creations among a transaction's actions, and to execution-context what code sees while running. protocol-deployment and deployment-launch are a label hazard, not a subject.
design.placements: One placement, L2 under smart-contracts; the label 'Deployment' is presentation, and opening on a contract's creation keeps the exposition from being read as protocol launch.

model.meaning: The values a smart contract platform supplies to code while it runs, beyond the call's input and the contract's storage, such as who made the call, which account started the transaction, what value arrived, the contract's own address, values of the current block and the metered resources left; each is set by some party and can be relied on only for what that party's role guarantees.

parents.smart-contracts: The parent states as a premise that what a contract knows about a call comes from its context and that relying on the original sender instead of the immediate caller can mislead. Start beyond it, do not restate it: which values there are, who sets each, why the originating account misleads (every contract on the path sees the same one; it can be a relayer), the block-producer and caller influence on block values and remaining resources, and how the values shift from call to call, including under a delegate-style call.

claims: what an execution environment exposes to running code beyond its input and storage, such as the immediate caller, the originating account, the value sent with the call, the contract's own address, block values and the remaining metered resources, and who sets each: the platform from the path of calls, the calling code for the value and resources it passes on, the transaction's sender through the transaction's fields, or, for block values, the protocol's rules and the block producer

what each context value can be trusted for: the immediate caller is set by the platform and cannot be chosen by the calling code, while the originating account names whoever signed or submitted the transaction, which every contract on the call path sees alike and which, where transactions are relayed or bundled, can be a relayer rather than the user; some block values are chosen or influenced by the block producer within bounds the protocol sets, so they are weak sources of fine-grained time and of randomness the producer cannot bias; and the remaining metered resources are what the caller chose to pass on, so code that branches on them can be steered by its caller

how what a callee sees changes along a chain of calls: the immediate caller and the value are set anew for each call, while the originating account stays fixed for the whole transaction, and so do block values where the whole chain of calls runs within one block, and a delegate-style call leaves the calling contract's caller, value and own address in place for the borrowed code, so a check that is sound in one call can mean something else in another

placements.execution-context: Only placement: L2 under Smart Contracts, which is platform-general. Write platform-general, with EVM names (msg.sender, tx.origin, msg.value, address(this), block values, gasleft) as examples, and hedge the values a platform may not expose. Nothing depends on wording placed elsewhere.

contents: Immediate caller: the account whose call started this invocation (the transaction's sender for the top-level call; the calling contract's address for a call issued by code).

Originating account: the account that signed the outer transaction (EVM tx.origin). Not every platform exposes it (CosmWasm exposes the immediate caller but not an origin); NEAR exposes both (predecessor vs signer).

Value sent with the call: only on platforms where a call carries native value (EVM, NEAR attached deposit); on others (Solana, Move chains) value moves as instructions or objects passed as input, so do not present it as universal.
Own address: the account the running code acts as and whose storage it runs against.
Block values: such as number, timestamp, a randomness value (EVM prevrandao), the producer's beneficiary address, chain id, base fee. Name the category; block-data owns block contents.
Remaining metered resources (EVM gasleft); name gas and metering, do not explain them.
Some platforms expose no immediate-caller value at all (Solana programs see accounts with signer flags, not the identity of a calling program); hedge 'exposes' accordingly.
producedBy: Platform, from the path of calls: immediate caller and own address (the call's target, or the caller's own address under a delegate-style call).

Calling code: value (in an ordinary call) and resources passed to a nested call, chosen by the caller within what it has and the platform's bounds (EVM: at most all but 1/64 of what remains; detail not needed). Note: the plan's claim 1 omits this setter; the record must not say the platform alone sets value or resources for nested calls.
Transaction's sender, through the transaction's fields: originating account (by signing), the top-level value and the top-level resource limit (gas limit).

Block values: some fixed by protocol rules (number, chain id, base fee computed from the parent), some chosen or influenced by the producer within protocol bounds (beneficiary; timestamp on chains that let the producer pick it within bounds; a randomness value the producer can bias, e.g. on Ethereum by withholding its block at the cost of its reward). Pitfall: on post-Merge Ethereum the timestamp follows the slot, so do not say every producer picks the timestamp freely; say 'chosen or influenced, within bounds, on many chains'.
checkedBy: The platform enforces what it sets: calling code cannot name another address as the caller; in an ordinary call the value really moved with the call (debited from the caller); under a delegate-style call it was not sent again; own address is the account executing.
The originating account is authenticated by the transaction signature the protocol checks; what that authenticates is who signed, not on whose behalf.

Nodes check block values against the protocol's rules (e.g. a timestamp later than the parent's; on Ethereum the randomness value against the mix in the chain's state, into which each proposer's signed reveal is mixed for the blocks after it); a value the rules accept is accepted whatever the producer's motive, so 'checked' means within bounds, not unbiased. Deterministic-execution owns how the values are made identical for every node: name only.
proves: Immediate caller: in an ordinary call, which account's code or signature made this call (under a delegate-style call the borrowed code sees the outer contract's caller instead). It does not establish that the caller acts for a particular user: a contract that forwards calls for anyone (a router, a relayer's forwarder) passes checks on its own address. Authorization and access-control: name only.

Originating account: who signed or submitted the outer transaction. Every contract on the call path reads the same value, so a contract the user calls, including a malicious one, can call onward while the origin still names the user; where transactions are relayed or bundled (meta-transactions, bundlers), it names the relayer or bundler. Relayers and account-abstraction: name only. Pitfall: do not present origin == caller as a reliable 'called directly by a user without code' test (since EIP-7702, May 2025, a signing account can carry code); if used, date it.

Value: that this amount arrived with this call, on platforms that carry value; under a delegate-style call the value was not sent again, so code that counts it per call can count one payment several times (well-known case: a batch function issuing delegate-style calls to itself, SushiSwap MISO, 2021; use only if dated and kept to the context effect).

Block values: coarse time and position in the chain; weak for fine-grained time (granularity is one block and producer-influenced where the producer can set it) and for randomness the producer cannot bias. Also, every transaction in the block reads the same value, and so does every contract in the transaction where its calls run within that block, so a calling contract can compute an outcome derived from it before acting and proceed only when it favors it; this is a second reason, not only producer bias. Timestamps owns timestamp reliability in oracle freshness: name only.

Remaining metered resources: only how much more this execution can do, which its caller decided; code that branches on it (or whose inner call can be starved while the outer code continues without checking) can be steered by the caller. Do not state gas costs or forwarding rules beyond naming.
lifetime: Set anew for each ordinary call: immediate caller, value, own address (to the target), remaining resources (to what the caller passes; then shrinks as code runs).

Fixed for the whole transaction: originating account. Block values: fixed where the whole chain of calls runs within one block (synchronous execution, as on EVM chains); on asynchronous platforms such as NEAR a called contract can run in a later block and read different block values. The plan's claim 3 lacks this condition; the record must carry it.

Delegate-style call: the borrowed code sees the calling contract's own caller, value and own address left in place. Name the call by this effect only; evm owns call kinds and what code runs against which storage.

Consequence: a check means what the context means at that call: a caller check in borrowed code tests the outer contract's caller; code can compare its own address with where it was deployed to detect being run as borrowed code. Do not overclaim that every check breaks; say a check sound in one call can test something else in another.
fields.variants: Platforms differ in which values they expose and how calls relate: EVM exposes both immediate caller and origin; NEAR both, with calls asynchronous across blocks; CosmWasm the immediate caller and funds but no origin; Solana no calling-program identity, with authority carried by signer accounts. Use at most one or two non-EVM contrasts and only to hedge generality; the claims are about values on platforms that expose them.

design.relationship: Six context values read across the same three questions the claims ask of each: who sets it, what it can be relied on for, and how it changes along a chain of calls. The reader's task is to read across values (which change per call and which stay fixed; which are platform-set versus caller- or producer-set) and down a value (what a given check on it establishes).

structures.purpose: The context values (immediate caller, originating account, value sent, own address, block values, remaining metered resources) as alternatives a contract might rely on, against three dimensions: set by, can be relied on for, along a chain of calls (including what a delegate-style call keeps).
