model.meaning: The phases a contract can pass through after deployment (in use, changed, disabled, removed), the transitions between them that its code or its platform provides, and what each transition does and does not change.

parents.smart-contracts: Parent premise (do not restate): deployment fixes code, many platforms cannot change it, upgradeability is added by design and its holder gains authority. This concept adds the phase view after deployment: which transitions a contract can have and where they come from (code or platform), which are reversible, the two ways of changing in effect (indirection vs migration) with what each keeps and what each leaves behind, and the limits of disabling and of removal (history, value sent afterward). Domain sentence on deployment vs lifecycle is a premise: deployment is entry and belongs to contract-deployment; this concept starts after it.

claims: the phases a deployed contract can pass through, in use, changed, disabled and removed, and why which transitions exist is a design choice fixed at deployment, though a provided upgrade path can add transitions later and renouncing an authority can remove them: short of a change to the platform's own rules, a transition is possible only if the contract's code or the platform provides it, so a contract that provides none can only be used or abandoned; some transitions can be reversed, as when a paused contract resumes, and others cannot

how a contract whose code cannot change is still changed in effect: routing calls through indirection to replaceable logic keeps the contract's address and, where the state lives at that address or in storage the replaceable logic does not own, its state, while migrating to a new contract leaves the old one in place and callable unless it is disabled, and requires users, integrations and state to move to the new address

what disabling or removing a contract can and cannot achieve: disabling stops chosen interactions, through the contract's own code or, on some platforms, a mechanism the platform provides, often leaving withdrawals open, while removal, where a platform permits it, deletes its code, and the state held in its own account, from the current state but not from the chain's history, so on a chain whose history is public past transactions and states stay readable wherever nodes or archives keep history, and value sent to a removed contract's address afterward can be lost; some platforms have restricted removal

placements.contract-lifecycle: Single L2 placement under Smart Contracts in Computation & Execution; the reader arrives from the parent's upgradeability paragraph. The exposition must stand on its own and stay platform-general, giving platform specifics only as hedged examples (some platforms, on EVM-style platforms).

actors: Whoever the contract's code grants a transition to (an admin key, a multisig, governance, sometimes anyone); upgrade-keys and timelocks named only, not explained.

The platform, where it provides a transition outside the contract's code: on some platforms a code-replacement or removal right is held by an authority set at deployment or by the account's keys (e.g. an upgrade authority or a contract admin); give at most one hedged example and no version detail.
Users and integrations (other contracts, front ends, approvals granted to the old address) who must move in a migration; anyone who later sends value to a removed contract's address.
assumptions: Premise in claim 1: 'short of a change to the platform's own rules'. A change to the platform's rules (named as protocol-upgrades, not explained) can alter any contract; keep that condition attached whenever saying a transition needs code or platform provision.

'Fixed at deployment' means the means of change are fixed then, not that the set of transitions can never move afterward: an upgrade path, if provided, can add transitions the original code lacked (e.g. a pause), and renouncing an authority can remove transitions for good. Do not write that the set of transitions is frozen forever.

Keeping state under indirection holds when the state lives at the fixed address and the replaceable logic runs against it (delegate-style), or in storage the replaceable logic does not own; state that lives in the replaced logic contract is not kept. Proxy mechanics belong to proxy-patterns: name, do not explain.

Disabling that the contract's own code provides is enforced by that code checking a flag or condition, so it covers only the paths that code checks; a disable a platform provides outside the code covers what the platform's rule covers; scope and granularity of pauses and the pause/unpause authority split belong to pause-mechanisms (named only).
outputs: Change in effect by indirection: same address, new behavior, and the state where it lives at that address or in storage the replaceable logic does not own; callers and integrations need not move.

Change in effect by migration: a new contract at a new address with its own lifecycle; the old contract stays deployed and callable with its state and holdings unless it is disabled or removed; users, integrations and state must move (state-migrations, migrations named only). Short of a change to the platform's rules, assets the old contract holds can leave only through paths its own code, or a transition the platform provides, allows; tokens recorded in other contracts' ledgers likewise need the old contract to call out unless those contracts grant someone else that power.

Disabling: chosen interactions refused by the contract's code, or by the platform where it provides a disable outside the code; a disable in the code leaves code, state and holdings in place and state as readable as it was, while a platform's disable keeps what its rule keeps; designs often keep withdrawals open so users can exit.

Removal, where permitted: code, and the state held in its own account, gone from the current state; state held outside it (balances in other contracts' ledgers, data in separate accounts where a platform keeps it there) can stay; past blocks, transactions and states remain in the chain's record and, on a chain whose history is public, stay readable from nodes or archives that keep history (pitfall: pruning nodes may not serve old state; do not say every node serves it).
failures: Value sent to a removed contract's address afterward: on EVM-style platforms the address becomes an account with no code and, in practice, no key anyone holds, so value sent there can be lost (say 'can be', not 'is': a later deployment at the same address could in principle release it); calls to it may succeed without running code (message-calls owns why; name only).
Migration leaves the old contract live: integrations still pointing at it, approvals granted to it and users who do not move keep using it, possibly with a known flaw, unless it is disabled.
A contract with no transitions cannot be repaired in place; its only options are continued use or abandonment (and a separate replacement contract, which is a migration, not a change to it).
A disable meant to be temporary can become permanent if the path that lifts it stops working; owned by pause-mechanisms, mention at most as a pointer.
states: In use (where a contract typically starts after deployment; some designs start disabled until set up), changed (replaced logic or code; not a distinct resting mode: after a change the contract is in use or disabled, with different behavior), disabled (temporary or permanent), removed (final for that contract's code and the state held in its own account).

Abandoned is not a phase of its own: where a platform charges nothing for keeping a contract and sets no lifetime on it, an abandoned contract stays deployed and callable; where it charges rent or lets state expire, an unpaid contract can be frozen, archived or deleted, a platform-provided transition (storage costs not explained).
transitions: Each transition exists only if the code or the platform provides it; which ones a given contract has differs per design and platform, so no single machine fits every contract.

Reversible: disabled to in use when the design provides a resume (a paused contract resumes); a change of logic can itself be changed again only through a provided change path (reverting is another upgrade; emergency-upgrades named only).

Irreversible: removal (the deleted state is not restored by the platform; pitfall: on some platforms a later deployment can place code at the same address again, which is a new contract, not a restoration; do not claim the address can never hold code again); renouncing an upgrade or pause authority, unless another retained authority, such as an upgrade path, can restore it; a permanent disable, which has no path back of its own, though a change path that remains can replace the logic enforcing it (kill-switches named only).
invariants: History is not changed by any lifecycle transition: earlier transactions and states stay in the chain's record.

A contract's own state is rewritten only through its code, a transition the platform provides, or a change to the platform's rules (parent premise; do not restate at length). Do not extend this to holdings: others can send it value.
variants: Removal by platform: on EVM-style platforms through an instruction the contract's own code must include (self-destruct), which Ethereum has restricted so that outside the creating transaction it no longer deletes code and state but still transfers the balance; other platforms offer account deletion or program closing by an authority. Write only 'some platforms have restricted removal' level detail with an example; no dates, versions, 'since' or 'recently'; no EIP numbers.
Change in effect: indirection (address and state kept, authority concentrated in whoever sets the target) vs migration (new address, old contract left live unless disabled, everything must move).
tradeoffs: Providing transitions (change, disable, removal) gives a response to flaws and changing needs but each is an authority someone holds over users; providing none gives users code that no one can change under them, short of a platform rule change, and no remedy other than abandoning it or migrating away (its behavior can still depend on contracts it calls; do not claim fixed behavior). State as a design trade-off, not a recommendation; do not restate the parent's trust sentence, and do not explain immutability (named only).

design.relationship: Conditions and consequences of transitions between post-deployment phases: each transition exists only where code or platform provides it, and each is characterized by what it keeps, removes or leaves behind (address, state, history, the old contract, value sent later).
design.whyProse: The concept has states and one return (a paused contract resumes), so a state block was considered and rejected. The claim's point is that the set of transitions differs per contract and platform; a state model draws one machine as if every contract had it, which misstates claim 1. 'Changed' is not a resting mode distinct from in use, and migration moves users to a second contract rather than moving one contract between states, so neither fits a single-contract state model. The one return is stated in a clause, and its conditions (who may pause and resume, how a pause becomes permanent) are pause-mechanisms' territory. Indirection versus migration is two alternatives a paragraph compares better than a two-row table, and removed-is-not-erased is one sentence, not a conflation needing a distinction block. The claims are arguments about conditions and consequences, which prose carries.
design.level: Lifecycle after deployment is this concept's own subject: the parent only states that code is fixed and upgradeability is added by design, and the specific transitions (pause, emergency upgrade, proxy, kill switch, migration) are separate concepts that each own their mechanism. This concept owns the phase view across them: where transitions come from, which reverse, and what change in effect, disabling and removal can and cannot achieve.
design.territory: Deployment (entry, initialization, addresses) stays with contract-deployment; persistence of code and data and layout compatibility with contract-state; why calls to a codeless account succeed with message-calls; how calls bind to replaceable code with contract-calls. Pause scope, authority split and stuck pauses stay with pause-mechanisms; fast-path upgrades and reverting with emergency-upgrades; proxy mechanics and their risks, upgrade keys, timelocks, immutability, migrations, state migrations, kill switches, protocol upgrades and deprecation are named only where a boundary is drawn.
design.placements: One placement (Computation & Execution / Smart Contracts / Contract Lifecycle); prose holds there and stays platform-general, with platform specifics only as hedged examples.

groupAudit.note: Group re-audit of smart-contracts (scoped to B1 of findings/group-smart-contracts.md), seven owned members read side by side with the parent; 0 group signals. B1 resolved: contract-execution P8 now reads 'Designs that commit each deferred call as an execution of its own, as NEAR does with each receipt, are the contrasting case: there an invocation's changes are committed when it finishes, and a later failure elsewhere does not undo them. 'Deferred call' is used in one sense in contract-execution and contract-calls. The pointer names Contract Calls without explaining dispatch, replies, submessages or compensation: no leakage.
